Below I justify the conclusion using precisely your authorized representative-selection facts, so acceptance does not depend on silently identifying those two notions.Two small presentation improvements would make the note more self-contained: specify the  $\mathbf F_2^3$  label order for the Heawood witness, and call  $N=2a+5$  “the first order not excluded by (3).” Neither changes the correctness verdict.1. Representative identities and pair ownershipWrite the bipartition as  $L\sqcup R$ , and let
$$A=T\cup V(M),\qquad B=V(G)\setminus A.$$
Because  $M$  is a matching, it has exactly  $m$  distinct endpoints in each part. Because  $T\cap V(M)=\varnothing$ , the identities
$$t_L+m+b_L=N,\qquad t_R+m+b_R=N$$
are exact.Combining them with
$$t_L+t_R+m=N+\delta$$
gives
$$t_R=b_L+\delta,\qquad t_L=b_R+\delta,\qquad
m+b_L+b_R=N-\delta.$$
These hold for  $\delta=0$  as well as for positive  $\delta$ . There is no factor-of-two error: matching endpoints contribute  $2m$  to the occupied vertex count, while matching edges contribute  $m$  to the objective.The ownership argument is valid in its full graph-to-cardinality form. For  $v\in T_R$ , feasibility and regularity give
$$d_{B_L}(v)=D-d_A(v)\ge D-1.$$
Define
$$\mathcal P_v=\binom{N(v)\cap B_L}{2}.$$
If distinct  $v,w\in T_R$  owned the same pair  $\{x,y\}$ , the vertices  $v,x,w,y$  would be four distinct vertices forming a four-cycle. Thus the sets  $\mathcal P_v$  are pairwise disjoint, and
$$\binom{D-1}{2}t_R
\le
\sum_{v\in T_R}\binom{d_{B_L}(v)}2
=
\left|\bigcup_{v\in T_R}\mathcal P_v\right|
\le
\binom{b_L}{2}.$$
The corresponding inequality on the other side follows independently.This addresses the ownership issue completely:Owners are vertices of  $T_R$ , or separately of  $T_L$ .Owned objects are unordered pairs in  $B_L$ , or separately in  $B_R$ .Matching endpoints belong to neither pair universe and are not owners.The two pair universes are disjoint because the bipartition classes are disjoint.The proof uses an ordinary matching, as defined. It does not require an induced matching, a maximal matching, or any degree restriction at matching endpoints.With  $a=(D-1)(D-2)>0$ , the resulting inequalities are exactly
$$a(b_L+\delta)\le b_L(b_L-1),\qquad
a(b_R+\delta)\le b_R(b_R-1).$$
2. Integer endpoints, the threshold, and the excess boundFor  $\delta\ge1$ , suppose an unused-side count satisfies  $0\le b\le a+1$ . Then
$$b(b-1)\le ab<a(b+\delta),$$
contradicting the packing inequality. This includes  $b=0$ : its right-hand side is zero, while  $a\delta>0$ .Since  $b$  is an integer, the conclusion is
$$b_L,b_R\ge a+2.$$
Consequently,
$$N=m+b_L+b_R+\delta\ge2a+5.$$
Therefore the stated hypothesis
$$N\le2a+4=2(D-1)(D-2)+4$$
excludes every objective exceeding  $N$ . The endpoint is handled correctly.A whole bipartition class is an independent set of size  $N$ , so the authorized inequalities yield
$$N\le\beta_2(G)\le\psi_{\rm sq}(G)\le\Omega(G)\le N.$$
This proves the theorem without enumeration or any formalization receipt. Connectedness plays no role. Equality of the part sizes follows from  $D|L|=D|R|$ , since  $D>0$ .The stronger excess estimate is also correct:
$$m+\delta=N-b_L-b_R\le N-2a-4.$$
For a positive-excess representative,
$$|T|+m=N+\delta\le2N-2a-4,$$
and representatives without positive excess have objective at most  $N$ . Hence
$$\Omega(G)\le\max\{N,\,2N-2a-4\}.$$
At  $N=2a+5$ , positive excess gives
$$m+\delta\le1.$$
The conditions  $m\ge0$ ,  $\delta\ge1$ , and integrality force
$$m=0,\qquad\delta=1.$$
When  $M=\varnothing$ , feasibility is exactly the condition that  $T$  is a dissociation set.The phrase “first possible order” is sound when read as “first order permitted by this bound.” The conditional statement does not establish existence at that order for every  $D$ ; the note supplies actual sharpness specifically for  $D=3$ .3. Equality-support rigidity and every projective planeAt objective exactly  $N$ , setting  $\delta=0$  gives
$$ab\le b(b-1).$$
Thus
$$b=0\quad\text{or}\quad b\ge a+1.$$

Suppose, for example, that  $b_L=0$ . Then
$$t_R=b_L=0.$$
It follows that:every vertex of  $L$  is occupied; $T\subseteq L$ ;every occupied vertex of  $R$  is a matching endpoint.This is exactly the claimed support orientation. The opposite orientation is symmetric.The case  $T=\varnothing$  is included. In that case, an objective- $N$  representative can be a perfect matching. Thus the note correctly refrains from forcing  $M=\varnothing$  in this equality regime. The claim concerns the support structure of every optimal representative pair; it does not assert that arbitrary pairs with this support shape automatically satisfy feasibility.For a finite projective plane of order  $q$ ,
$$N=q^2+q+1,\qquad D=q+1,\qquad a=q(q-1).$$
The projective-plane incidence axiom excludes a four-cycle, because two distinct points cannot lie on two distinct common lines.The theorem’s size margin is

Writing  $q=2+k$ ,  $k\ge0$ , gives

Therefore
$$\beta_2=\psi_{\rm sq}=\Omega=q^2+q+1$$
for every finite projective plane of order  $q\ge2$ .For the stronger support conclusion,

\iff
q^2+q+1\le2q(q-1)+1

q(q-3)\ge0.$$
Within  $q\ge2$ , this holds exactly for  $q\ge3$ .
